title: Ἀγαμέμνονος ψυχή
titleEn: The Pause in the Tale and Agamemnon’s Soul — Odyssey 11.321–434
part: The Pause in the Tale and Agamemnon’s Soul (11.321–434)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus finishes naming the great women of the dead, then breaks off: he says he could not name them all, and that it is time to sleep. The hall falls silent, spellbound. Queen Arete asks the Phaeacians what they think of such a guest and urges them not to send him off early or stint his gifts, the old Echeneus agrees, and Alcinous promises that Odysseus will have his escort but asks him to stay one more day. Odysseus says he would gladly stay even a year, for the gifts and the honour at home. Alcinous praises him as no cheat but a man who tells his tale like a minstrel, and asks whether he saw any of his companions from Troy. Odysseus agrees to go on, and tells how the soul of Agamemnon came up among those who died with him in the house of Aegisthus. Weeping, the king could not touch him. Odysseus asks how he died, and Agamemnon answers that it was neither storm nor battle but Aegisthus, at a feast, with his wife; he describes the slaughter in the hall, the death of Cassandra, and how Clytemnestra would not even close his eyes, and ends in bitterness against all women.

sentences.t:
Φαίδρην τε Πρόκριν τε ἴδον καλήν τ’ Ἀριάδνην,
κούρην Μίνωος ὀλοόφρονος, ἥν ποτε Θησεὺς
ἐκ Κρήτης ἐς γουνὸν Ἀθηνάων ἱεράων
ἦγε μέν, οὐδ’ ἀπόνητο·
sentences.tr:
Phaidrēn te Prokrin te idon kalēn t’ Ariadnēn,
kourēn Minōos oloophronos, hēn pote Thēseus
ek Krētēs es gounon Athēnaōn hieraōn
ēge men, oud’ aponēto·
sentences.l:
Phaedra and Procris I saw, and fine Ariadne,
daughter of baleful-minded Minos, whom once Theseus
from Crete to the rising ground of sacred Athens
was leading, yet had no enjoyment of her;
sentences.i: I saw Phaedra and Procris and beautiful Ariadne, the daughter of baleful-minded Minos, whom Theseus was once taking from Crete to the rising ground of sacred Athens, but he had no enjoyment of her;
sentences.n: The three names are all objects of ἴδον, the aorist of ὁράω without its augment (Attic εἶδον): Homer’s past tenses may lack the ἐ-. τε … τε … τ’ joins them, ‘both … and … and’. The relative clause belongs to Ariadne: ἥν is ‘whom’, and ὀλοόφρονος, ‘baleful-minded’ (ὀλοός ‘deadly’ + φρήν), is the epithet of her father Minos. ἐς γουνὸν Ἀθηνάων ἱεράων is ‘to the rising ground of sacred Athens’: γουνός is ‘rising ground, hill’, Ἀθηνάων the genitive plural of the plural name Ἀθῆναι. ἀπόνητο is the aorist middle of ἀπονίναμαι ‘have profit or enjoyment of’: ‘he was taking her, but had no enjoyment of her’.

sentences.t:
πάρος δέ μιν Ἄρτεμις ἔκτα
Δίῃ ἐν ἀμφιρύτῃ Διονύσου μαρτυρίῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
paros de min Artemis ekta
Diēi en amphirytēi Dionysou martyriēisin.
sentences.l:
but before that Artemis killed her
in flowed-around Dia, on Dionysus’ testimony.
sentences.i: but before that Artemis killed her in Dia, with the sea running all round it, on the testimony of Dionysus.
sentences.n: What happened to Ariadne before Theseus could enjoy her. πάρος δέ is ‘but before (that)’, and ἔκτα is the aorist of κτείνω ‘kill’ in its short athematic form, with the augment (the longer form is ἔκτανε). Δίῃ is Dia, an island by the sense of its epithet: ἀμφιρύτῃ is ‘flowed around’ (ἀμφί ‘around’ + ῥέω ‘flow’), so water on every side; ἐν stands between the noun and its adjective. Διονύσου μαρτυρίῃσιν is a dative plural, ‘on the testimony of Dionysus’, a plural noun where English has a singular. The Greek does not say what Dionysus testified, and the translation does not guess.

sentences.t:
Μαῖράν τε Κλυμένην τε ἴδον στυγερήν τ’ Ἐριφύλην,
ἣ χρυσὸν φίλου ἀνδρὸς ἐδέξατο τιμήεντα.
sentences.tr:
Mairan te Klymenēn te idon stygerēn t’ Eriphylēn,
hē chryson philou andros edexato timēenta.
sentences.l:
Maera and Clymene I saw, and hateful Eriphyle,
who gold for her dear husband accepted, precious.
sentences.i: I saw Maera and Clymene and hateful Eriphyle, who accepted precious gold as the price of her dear husband.
sentences.n: Three more names, only the last of which gets a clause of story. Μαῖραν and Κλυμένην are bare names; Ἐριφύλην is στυγερήν ‘hateful’. The relative clause ἣ χρυσὸν … ἐδέξατο τιμήεντα is ‘who accepted precious gold’, with ἐδέξατο the aorist middle of δέχομαι ‘accept’; τιμήεντα is built on τιμή ‘value, honour’ and means ‘valued, precious’. The genitive φίλου ἀνδρός says what the gold was the price of, ‘for her dear husband’; the husband is not named in these lines.

sentences.t:
πάσας δ’ οὐκ ἂν ἐγὼ μυθήσομαι οὐδ’ ὀνομήνω,
ὅσσας ἡρώων ἀλόχους ἴδον ἠδὲ θύγατρας·
sentences.tr:
pasas d’ ouk an egō mythēsomai oud’ onomēnō,
hossas hērōōn alochous idon ēde thygatras·
sentences.l:
And all of them I could not tell or name,
as many as I saw of heroes’ wives and daughters;
sentences.i: I could not tell or name them all, all the wives and daughters of heroes that I saw;
sentences.n: Odysseus says he cannot name them all. οὐκ ἂν … μυθήσομαι οὐδ’ ὀνομήνω is ‘I could not tell, nor name’: ἄν (the κε of other lines) with a subjunctive gives a ‘could’, and μυθήσομαι, which looks like a future, and ὀνομήνω are most likely aorist subjunctives of μυθέομαι and ὀνομαίνω. πάσας ‘all’ is taken up by ὅσσας … ἴδον ‘as many as I saw’. ἡρώων is the genitive plural of ἥρως ‘hero’, ἀλόχους is ‘wives’, and ἠδέ is ‘and’ (= καί). The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t: πρὶν γάρ κεν καὶ νὺξ φθῖτ’ ἄμβροτος.
sentences.tr: prin gar ken kai nyx phthit’ ambrotos.
sentences.l: for sooner would even the night perish, deathless.
sentences.i: for even the night, deathless though it is, would be spent before I finished.
sentences.n: Why he must stop: the night would give out first. φθῖτ’ is φθῖτο, the aorist optative middle of φθίνω ‘waste away, perish’, and with κεν it is a ‘would’: ‘would perish’. πρίν is here the adverb ‘sooner, before that’, not the conjunction. ἄμβροτος ‘deathless’ is the word for what does not die; applied to night it is the point of the exaggeration. The full stop falls in the middle of the line, so the unit ends there and ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥρη opens the next.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὥρη
εὕδειν, ἢ ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν ἐλθόντ’ ἐς ἑταίρους
ἢ αὐτοῦ·
sentences.tr:
alla kai hōrē
heudein, ē epi nēa thoēn elthont’ es hetairous
ē autou·
sentences.i: But it is also time to sleep, whether I go to the swift ship and my companions or stay here;
sentences.n: A second reason to stop, and a choice of where to sleep. ὥρη (understand ἐστί) εὕδειν is ‘it is time to sleep’, and ἢ … ἢ … is ‘either … or’. ἐλθόντ’ is ἐλθόντα, an accusative participle agreeing with an unspoken ‘me’: ‘time for me, having gone’. νῆα θοήν is ‘the swift ship’, and ἐς ἑταίρους ‘to my companions’ says that the men are with the ship. αὐτοῦ is the fixed adverb ‘there, on the spot’, here ‘here’.

sentences.t: πομπὴ δὲ θεοῖς ὑμῖν τε μελήσει.
sentences.tr: pompē de theois hymin te melēsei.
sentences.l: and my escort will be a care to the gods and to you.”
sentences.i: and my escort will be the concern of the gods and of you.”
sentences.n: He ends by handing the matter of his escort home to the hosts. πομπή is the sending-off, ‘escort’; μελήσει is the future of μέλω ‘be a care to’, which takes the dative, here θεοῖς ὑμῖν τε ‘to the gods and to you’. The closing quotation mark is placed here because the narrator speaks in the next line: the long speech Odysseus has been making to the Phaeacians (opened at 9.2) ends with this unit.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ,
κηληθμῷ δ’ ἔσχοντο κατὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi,
kēlēthmōi d’ eschonto kata megara skioenta.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence,
and were held by a spell throughout the shadowy halls.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent, held in a spell throughout the shadowy halls.
sentences.n: The narrator’s voice returns for a moment: Odysseus has stopped. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ὣς ἔφατο, ‘so he spoke’, with the τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of οἱ; οἱ here is ‘they’, the old demonstrative pronoun that later became the article. ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ is the set phrase ‘became still in silence’. κηληθμῷ is the dative of κηληθμός ‘spell, enchantment’ (from κηλέω ‘charm’), and ἔσχοντο, the aorist middle of ἔχω, is passive in sense: ‘were held’. κατὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα is ‘throughout the shadowy halls’ (σκιόεις from σκιά ‘shadow’).

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀρήτη λευκώλενος ἤρχετο μύθων.
sentences.tr: toisin d’ Arētē leukōlenos ērcheto mythōn.
sentences.l: and among them white-armed Arete began the talk:
sentences.i: Then white-armed Arete began to speak among them:
sentences.n: Arete, Alcinous’s queen, is the first to answer the silence. τοῖσιν is the dative plural of the pronoun, ‘among them’; ἤρχετο is the imperfect of ἄρχομαι ‘begin’, which takes the genitive, μύθων ‘of the talk’. λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is her epithet here (λευκός ‘white’ + ὠλένη ‘forearm’).

sentences.t:
Φαίηκες, πῶς ὔμμιν ἀνὴρ ὅδε φαίνεται εἶναι
εἶδός τε μέγεθός τε ἰδὲ φρένας ἔνδον ἐίσας;
sentences.tr:
Phaiēkes, pōs ymmin anēr hode phainetai einai
eidos te megethos te ide phrenas endon eisas;
sentences.l:
“Phaeacians, how to you does this man appear to be
in looks and in stature and in the wits within, well-balanced?
sentences.i: “Phaeacians, how does this man appear to you, in looks and stature, and in the well-balanced mind within?
sentences.n: Arete asks the court what they make of the stranger. Φαίηκες is a vocative plural; ὔμμιν is an epic form of ὑμῖν ‘to you’; πῶς … φαίνεται εἶναι is ‘how does he appear to be’. Three accusatives answer ‘in what respect’: εἶδος ‘looks’, μέγεθος ‘stature’, φρένας ‘wits’. φρένας ἔνδον ἐίσας is ‘the wits within, well-balanced’; the sense of ἐίσας (from the same word as ‘equal, even’) is not certain, and ‘well-balanced’ is the traditional guess. The question ends in the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: ξεῖνος δ’ αὖτ’ ἐμός ἐστιν, ἕκαστος δ’ ἔμμορε τιμῆς·
sentences.tr: xeinos d’ aut’ emos estin, hekastos d’ emmore timēs·
sentences.l: And a guest-friend, moreover, mine he is, and each has a share of honour;
sentences.i: Moreover he is my guest-friend, and each of you has a share of honour;
sentences.n: She claims him as her guest and, in the same breath, shares the honour of it. ξεῖνος is the guest-friend, the man bound to a host, and ἐμός ‘mine’ makes him hers; δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘and moreover’. ἔμμορε is the perfect of μείρομαι ‘get a share of’, which takes the genitive: τιμῆς ‘of honour’. Which honour is meant (that of having him as a guest, most likely) the Greek does not say.

sentences.t:
τῷ μὴ ἐπειγόμενοι ἀποπέμπετε, μηδὲ τὰ δῶρα
οὕτω χρηίζοντι κολούετε·
sentences.tr:
tōi mē epeigomenoi apopempete, mēde ta dōra
houtō chrēizonti kolouete·
sentences.l:
therefore do not, pressing on, send him away, nor the gifts
to one so in need curtail;
sentences.i: So do not be hasty in sending him off, and do not cut short the gifts for a man in such need;
sentences.n: Her first request: do not hurry him away or cut his gifts short. τῷ is an old instrumental of the pronoun, ‘therefore, so’. μή with a present imperative (ἀποπέμπετε, κολούετε) is a prohibition, ‘do not send away, do not curtail’; ἐπειγόμενοι is ‘pressing on, in haste’. κολούετε is ‘cut short, dock’. χρηίζοντι is a dative participle of χρηίζω ‘need’, ‘to one so in need’ (of them), and οὕτω is ‘so’. The ano teleia ends the unit before her reason.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ γὰρ ὑμῖν
κτήματ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισι θεῶν ἰότητι κέονται.
sentences.tr:
polla gar hymin
ktēmat’ eni megaroisi theōn iotēti keontai.
sentences.l:
for many to you
possessions in the halls, by the gods’ will, lie.”
sentences.i: for many possessions lie in your halls, by the will of the gods.”
sentences.n: Her reason: there is plenty. πολλὰ … κτήματα is ‘many possessions’ with ὑμῖν ‘for you’; κέονται is the epic form of κεῖνται ‘lie’. μεγάροισι has the dative ending -οισι and ἐνί stands for ἐν. θεῶν ἰότητι is ‘by the will of the gods’: ἰότης is ‘will, goodwill’, and the dative gives the cause. Arete’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε γέρων ἥρως Ἐχένηος,
ὃς δὴ Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν προγενέστερος ἦεν·
sentences.tr:
toisi de kai meteeipe gerōn hērōs Echenēos,
hos dē Phaiēkōn andrōn progenesteros ēen·
sentences.l:
And among them spoke also the old hero Echeneus,
who indeed of the Phaeacian men was the elder;
sentences.i: And among them the old hero Echeneus spoke up as well, who was the elder of the Phaeacian men;
sentences.n: A second voice joins Arete’s. τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε is ‘and among them spoke also’: μετέειπε is ‘spoke among’, and καί says that this is another speaker after the queen. γέρων ἥρως ‘the old hero’ gives Echeneus his title (ἥρως is used of a man of standing). ὃς δὴ … προγενέστερος ἦεν is ‘who was indeed the elder’: προγενέστερος is a comparative, ‘born earlier’, with the partitive genitive Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν, and ἦεν is the epic imperfect of εἰμί.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐ μὰν ἧμιν ἀπὸ σκοποῦ οὐδ’ ἀπὸ δόξης
μυθεῖται βασίλεια περίφρων·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi, ou man hēmin apo skopou oud’ apo doxēs
mytheitai basileia periphrōn·
sentences.l:
“Friends, not truly to us wide of the mark nor away from opinion
speaks the queen, circumspect;
sentences.i: “Friends, the circumspect queen does not speak to us wide of the mark, or at odds with what we think;
sentences.n: Echeneus backs the queen. ὦ φίλοι is ‘friends’; ἧμιν is the epic ἡμῖν ‘to us’; οὐ μάν is ‘truly not’. ἀπὸ σκοποῦ is ‘off the mark’ (σκοπός ‘target’). ἀπὸ δόξης is less clear: δόξα is ‘opinion’ or ‘expectation’, so the phrase is either ‘at odds with what we think’ or ‘against what we expect’, and the translation takes the first. μυθεῖται is the contracted present of μυθέομαι ‘speak’, and βασίλεια περίφρων is ‘the circumspect queen’, with περίφρων ‘careful in mind’ (περί + φρήν).

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ πίθεσθε.
sentences.tr: alla pithesthe.
sentences.l: but obey.
sentences.i: so do as she says.
sentences.n: The conclusion in two words. πίθεσθε is the aorist middle imperative of πείθομαι ‘obey, be persuaded’, so ‘take her advice’. ἀλλά is ‘but’ in the sense ‘all the same, then’.

sentences.t: Ἀλκινόου δ’ ἐκ τοῦδ’ ἔχεται ἔργον τε ἔπος τε.
sentences.tr: Alkinoou d’ ek toud’ echetai ergon te epos te.
sentences.l: And on Alcinous, from this, depends both deed and word.”
sentences.i: And from here on, both action and word rest with Alcinous.”
sentences.n: He hands the decision to the king. ἔργον τε ἔπος τε is ‘both deed and word’, and ἔχεται, from ἔχομαι ‘hold on to, depend on’, takes the genitive Ἀλκινόου. ἐκ τοῦδ’ can be ‘from this man’ or ‘from now on’, and the translation takes the second; the first would give ‘both deed and word hang from Alcinous here’. Echeneus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀλκίνοος ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Alkinoos apameibeto phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: Him then in turn answered Alcinous, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and spoke:
sentences.n: A reply-formula: τὸν is ‘him’ (the pronoun, not the article), αὖτ’ is ‘in turn’, ἀπαμείβετο is the imperfect middle of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’, and φώνησέν τε adds ‘and spoke’. The same line opens each of Alcinous’s replies in this part.

sentences.t:
τοῦτο μὲν οὕτω δὴ ἔσται ἔπος, αἴ κεν ἐγώ γε
ζωὸς Φαιήκεσσι φιληρέτμοισιν ἀνάσσω·
sentences.tr:
touto men houtō dē estai epos, ai ken egō ge
zōos Phaiēkessi philēretmoisin anassō·
sentences.l:
“This word, indeed, shall be so, if I at least
alive over the oar-loving Phaeacians rule;
sentences.i: “This word shall stand just so, as long as I live and rule over the oar-loving Phaeacians;
sentences.n: Alcinous accepts what has just been said. τοῦτο … ἔπος is ‘this word’, the advice of Echeneus and Arete, and ἔσται is ‘shall be’. αἴ κεν ἐγώ γε … ἀνάσσω is ‘if I at least rule’: αἴ is an epic form of εἰ, and κεν takes the subjunctive ἀνάσσω. ζωός is ‘alive’. ἀνάσσω takes the dative, Φαιήκεσσι φιληρέτμοισιν, with the -εσσι and -οισιν endings, ‘over the oar-loving Phaeacians’. ἐγώ γε stresses that it is his own authority he is relying on.

sentences.t:
ξεῖνος δὲ τλήτω μάλα περ νόστοιο χατίζων
ἔμπης οὖν ἐπιμεῖναι ἐς αὔριον, εἰς ὅ κε πᾶσαν
δωτίνην τελέσω·
sentences.tr:
xeinos de tlētō mala per nostoio chatizōn
empēs oun epimeinai es aurion, eis ho ke pasan
dōtinēn telesō·
sentences.i: and let the stranger bring himself, much as he wants his homecoming, to stay on nevertheless until tomorrow, until I have completed the whole gift;
sentences.n: He asks Odysseus to stay one more day. τλήτω is the aorist imperative of τλάω ‘endure, bring oneself to’, so ‘let him bring himself … to stay’, with the infinitive ἐπιμεῖναι ‘to remain’. μάλα περ νόστοιο χατίζων is concessive, ‘very much though he wants his homecoming’; χατίζω ‘want, need’ takes the genitive. ἔμπης οὖν is ‘nevertheless, then’. εἰς ὅ κε … τελέσω is ‘until I complete’, with κε and the aorist subjunctive. δωτίνη is ‘gift’, and πᾶσαν δωτίνην is the gift in full.

sentences.t:
πομπὴ δ’ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει
πᾶσι, μάλιστα δ’ ἐμοί·
sentences.tr:
pompē d’ andressi melēsei
pasi, malista d’ emoi·
sentences.l:
and the escort will be a care to the men,
to all, and most of all to me;
sentences.i: and his escort will be the care of all the men, and most of all my own;
sentences.n: Who is responsible for the escort. μελήσει repeats the verb Odysseus used of his own escort a few lines earlier, now with the Phaeacians as the ones who will care: ἄνδρεσσι πᾶσι is ‘for all the men’ (the dative ending -εσσι again), and μάλιστα δ’ ἐμοί is ‘and most of all for me’. The ano teleia ends the unit before the reason.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ κράτος ἔστ’ ἐνὶ δήμῳ.
sentences.tr: tou gar kratos est’ eni dēmōi.
sentences.l: for of him the power is in the land.”
sentences.i: for the power in the land is mine.”
sentences.n: The reason, in a compressed line. τοῦ is the pronoun ‘of him’, and it points back to ἐμοί, the speaker himself: ‘for his is the power’; the translation puts it in the first person. ἔστ’ is ἔστι, and ἐνί is ἐν. κράτος is ‘power, rule’, and δῆμος the land with its people, ‘land’ in both layers. Alcinous’s speech ends.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: Another reply-formula, this time for Odysseus. τὸν is ‘him’ (the pronoun, not the article), ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’, and προσέφη is ‘addressed’, the aorist of πρόσφημι. πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ is Odysseus’s standing epithet (μῆτις ‘cunning intelligence’).

sentences.t:
Ἀλκίνοε κρεῖον, πάντων ἀριδείκετε λαῶν,
εἴ με καὶ εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν ἀνώγοιτ’ αὐτόθι μίμνειν,
πομπὴν δ’ ὀτρύνοιτε καὶ ἀγλαὰ δῶρα διδοῖτε,
sentences.tr:
Alkinoe kreion, pantōn arideikete laōn,
ei me kai eis eniauton anōgoit’ autothi mimnein,
pompēn d’ otrynoite kai aglaa dōra didoite,
sentences.i: “Alcinous, my lord, most distinguished of all the people, if you were to bid me stay here even for a year, and were to speed my escort and give me splendid gifts,
sentences.n: Odysseus answers with a conditional, and the condition fills three lines. κρεῖον is the vocative of κρείων ‘lord’, and ἀριδείκετε is the vocative of ἀριδείκετος ‘most conspicuous, most distinguished’. The verbs ἀνώγοιτ’ (for ἀνώγοιτε), ὀτρύνοιτε and διδοῖτε are plural optatives, ‘if you all were to bid, urge, give’: Alcinous is addressed, but the Phaeacians as a body are meant. εἰς ἐνιαυτόν is ‘for a year’, αὐτόθι ‘right here’, and ἀγλαά ‘splendid’. The sentence runs five lines; the comma after διδοῖτε is where the syntax pauses most, between the condition and the clause that answers it.

sentences.t:
καί κε τὸ βουλοίμην, καί κεν πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη,
πλειοτέρῃ σὺν χειρὶ φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἱκέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
kai ke to bouloimēn, kai ken poly kerdion eiē,
pleioterēi syn cheiri philēn es patrid’ hikesthai·
sentences.l:
even that I should wish, and much better it would be,
with a fuller hand to my dear fatherland to come;
sentences.i: I should wish even that, and it would be far better to come to my dear fatherland with a fuller hand;
sentences.n: What he would say to the offer of a year. καί κε τὸ βουλοίμην is ‘I would wish even that’, κε with the optative; καί κεν πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη is ‘and it would be much better’. κέρδιον is the comparative of κέρδος ‘gain, profit’, so the thought is ‘more to my advantage’, and ‘better’ is the translation. πλειοτέρῃ σὺν χειρί is ‘with a fuller hand’: more in the hand, that is, more gifts. φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ is ‘to my dear fatherland’, and ἱκέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to, reach’. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
καί κ’ αἰδοιότερος καὶ φίλτερος ἀνδράσιν εἴην
πᾶσιν, ὅσοι μ’ Ἰθάκηνδε ἰδοίατο νοστήσαντα.
sentences.tr:
kai k’ aidoioteros kai philteros andrasin eiēn
pasin, hosoi m’ Ithakēnde idoiato nostēsanta.
sentences.l:
and more revered and dearer would I be to men
all, as many as might see me come home to Ithaca.”
sentences.i: and I should be the more revered, and dearer, to all the men who might see me come home to Ithaca.”
sentences.n: The reward he names: standing at home. καί κ’ … εἴην is again κε with the optative, ‘I would be’. αἰδοιότερος and φίλτερος are comparatives of αἰδοῖος ‘revered’ and φίλος ‘dear’, with the dative ἀνδράσιν πᾶσιν ‘to all men’. ὅσοι μ’ … ἰδοίατο is ‘as many as might see me’, an aorist middle optative; Ἰθάκηνδε is ‘to Ithaca’ with the -δε of direction, and νοστήσαντα is the aorist participle of νοστέω ‘come home’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀλκίνοος ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Alkinoos apameibeto phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: Him then in turn answered Alcinous, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Alcinous answered him in turn, and spoke:
sentences.n: Alcinous answers again with the line that opened his earlier reply: τὸν is ‘him’, αὖτ’ ‘in turn’, and ἀπαμείβετο ‘answered’, so the same words introduce each of his replies in this part.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ὀδυσεῦ, τὸ μὲν οὔ τί σ’ ἐίσκομεν εἰσορόωντες,
ἠπεροπῆά τ’ ἔμεν καὶ ἐπίκλοπον, οἷά τε πολλοὺς
βόσκει γαῖα μέλαινα πολυσπερέας ἀνθρώπους,
ψεύδεά τ’ ἀρτύνοντας ὅθεν κέ τις οὐδὲ ἴδοιτο·
sentences.tr:
ō Odyseu, to men ou ti s’ eiskomen eisoroōntes,
ēperopēa t’ emen kai epiklopon, hoia te pollous
boskei gaia melaina polyspereas anthrōpous,
pseudea t’ artynontas hothen ke tis oude idoito·
sentences.l:
“O Odysseus, in this at least we do not liken you, looking upon you,
to be a deceiver and a thievish one, such as many
the dark earth feeds, men widely scattered,
fashioning lies, whence one might not even see;
sentences.i: “Odysseus, looking at you we do not take you to be a deceiver and a trickster, of the kind the dark earth feeds in great numbers, men scattered far and wide, who fashion lies from sources no one could even see;
sentences.n: Alcinous says what Odysseus is not. Ὀδυσεῦ is the vocative with a single σ, beside Ὀδυσσεῦ. τὸ μέν is ‘in this respect’, and ἐίσκομεν, from ἐΐσκω ‘liken, suppose’, makes ‘we do not suppose’. ἠπεροπῆα and ἐπίκλοπον, with ἔμεν (= εἶναι), are ‘a deceiver and a thievish one’ (ἐπίκλοπος ‘sly’). οἷά τε is ‘of the kind that’, with the epic τε of general truths; πολυσπερέας is ‘widely scattered’. ψεύδεα … ἀρτύνοντας is ‘fashioning lies’. The last clause, ὅθεν κέ τις οὐδὲ ἴδοιτο, literally ‘whence one might not even see’, is compressed: it seems to mean lies from a source nobody could look at, but the sense is not certain.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ ἔπι μὲν μορφὴ ἐπέων, ἔνι δὲ φρένες ἐσθλαί.
sentences.tr: soi d’ epi men morphē epeōn, eni de phrenes esthlai.
sentences.l: but on you is a shape of words, and within are good wits.
sentences.i: but your words have a shapely grace, and good sense lies within.
sentences.n: What Odysseus is instead. ἔπι and ἔνι stand for ἔπεστι and ἔνεστι, ‘is on’ and ‘is in’; the accent is thrown back on a preposition that stands for the verb. μορφὴ ἐπέων is ‘a shape of words’, the graceful form his words take, and φρένες ἐσθλαί are ‘good wits’ (ἐσθλός ‘good’). σοί is ‘on you’.

sentences.t:
μῦθον δ’ ὡς ὅτ’ ἀοιδὸς ἐπισταμένως κατέλεξας,
πάντων τ’ Ἀργείων σέο τ’ αὐτοῦ κήδεα λυγρά.
sentences.tr:
mython d’ hōs hot’ aoidos epistamenōs katelexas,
pantōn t’ Argeiōn seo t’ autou kēdea lygra.
sentences.l:
And the tale, as when a minstrel, skilfully you recounted,
of all the Argives and of yourself the grievous sorrows.
sentences.i: You have told your tale as skilfully as a minstrel, the grievous sorrows of all the Argives and of yourself.
sentences.n: He compares Odysseus to a singer. μῦθον … κατέλεξας is ‘you recounted the tale’, from καταλέγω ‘tell in full’, and ὡς ὅτ’ ἀοιδός is ‘as when a minstrel (does)’; ἐπισταμένως is ‘knowingly, with skill’. Ἀργείων is ‘of the Argives’, the poet’s name for the Greeks as a whole, and σέο is σοῦ, ‘of you’, with αὐτοῦ ‘yourself’. κήδεα λυγρά is ‘grievous sorrows’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
εἴ τινας ἀντιθέων ἑτάρων ἴδες, οἵ τοι ἅμ’ αὐτῷ
Ἴλιον εἰς ἅμ’ ἕποντο καὶ αὐτοῦ πότμον ἐπέσπον.
sentences.tr:
all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon,
ei tinas antitheōn hetarōn ides, hoi toi ham’ autōi
Ilion eis ham’ heponto kai autou potmon epespon.
sentences.l:
But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly,
if any of your godlike companions you saw, who along with you yourself
to Ilios followed, and there met their doom.
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly: whether you saw any of your godlike companions, who went with you to Ilios and met their doom there.
sentences.n: The question Alcinous wants answered. ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον is the fixed ‘but come, tell me this, and recount it exactly’; here the line ends in a comma, because the question follows. εἰ … ἴδες is an indirect question, ‘whether you saw’, with the unaugmented aorist ἴδες. ἀντιθέων ἑτάρων is ‘godlike companions’. οἵ τοι ἅμ’ αὐτῷ … ἕποντο is ‘who followed along with you yourself’: τοι is the epic σοι ‘to you’, αὐτῷ the intensifier, ἕποντο the imperfect of ἕπομαι. Ἴλιον is Troy. καὶ αὐτοῦ πότμον ἐπέσπον is ‘and there met their doom’: αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘there’, and ἐπέσπον, the aorist of ἐφέπω, ‘came upon’.

sentences.t: νὺξ δ’ ἥδε μάλα μακρή,
sentences.tr: nyx d’ hēde mala makrē,
sentences.l: And this night is very long,
sentences.i: This night is very long,
sentences.n: Why he wants the tale now. ἥδε is ‘this (night here)’, and μάλα ‘very’; μακρή ‘long’ is the predicate. The next word, ἀθέσφατος, is the first word of the following unit, which comments on it.

sentences.t:
ἀθέσφατος· οὐδέ πω ὥρη
εὕδειν ἐν μεγάρῳ, σὺ δέ μοι λέγε θέσκελα ἔργα.
sentences.tr:
athesphatos· oude pō hōrē
heudein en megarōi, sy de moi lege theskela erga.
sentences.l:
immense; and not yet is it time
to sleep in the hall; but you, tell me marvellous deeds.
sentences.i: immense, and it is not yet time to sleep in the hall; so tell me of marvellous deeds.
sentences.n: ἀθέσφατος, said of the night, is traditionally ‘immense’, explained as ‘beyond what a god has declared’, that is beyond telling or measure; that explanation is a guess, and the sense of the word is not certain. οὐδέ πω ὥρη (understand ἐστί) is ‘nor is it yet time’, with εὕδειν ‘to sleep’ and the singular ἐν μεγάρῳ ‘in the hall’. σὺ δέ μοι λέγε is ‘but you, tell me’, a present imperative. θέσκελα ἔργα is ‘marvellous deeds’: the meaning of θέσκελος is not known, and ‘marvellous’ is the traditional guess, perhaps from θεός ‘god’.

sentences.t:
καί κεν ἐς ἠῶ δῖαν ἀνασχοίμην, ὅτε μοι σὺ
τλαίης ἐν μεγάρῳ τὰ σὰ κήδεα μυθήσασθαι.
sentences.tr:
kai ken es ēō dian anaschoimēn, hote moi sy
tlaiēs en megarōi ta sa kēdea mythēsasthai.
sentences.l:
And even to heavenly dawn I would hold out, if you to me
were to bring yourself in the hall to tell your sorrows.”
sentences.i: I could hold out even until heavenly dawn, if you could bring yourself to tell me of your sorrows here in the hall.”
sentences.n: He offers to stay up all night. κεν … ἀνασχοίμην is ‘I would hold out’, the aorist optative middle of ἀνέχω. ἐς ἠῶ δῖαν is ‘until heavenly dawn’, with ἠῶ the accusative of ἠώς and δῖαν the ‘heavenly’ of divine things. ὅτε … τλαίης is ‘when you could bring yourself’, with the aorist optative of τλάω (compare τλήτω above), and ὅτε with the optative has here the force ‘if ever’; τὰ σὰ κήδεα μυθήσασθαι is ‘to tell your own sorrows’. Alcinous’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: The same reply-formula as before: τὸν ‘him’, ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’, προσέφη ‘addressed’, with πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’. It now introduces Odysseus’s answer to the question about his companions.

sentences.t:
Ἀλκίνοε κρεῖον, πάντων ἀριδείκετε λαῶν,
ὥρη μὲν πολέων μύθων, ὥρη δὲ καὶ ὕπνου·
sentences.tr:
Alkinoe kreion, pantōn arideikete laōn,
hōrē men poleōn mythōn, hōrē de kai hypnou·
sentences.l:
“Alcinous, lord, most conspicuous of all the people,
a time for many tales, and a time too for sleep;
sentences.i: “Alcinous, my lord, most distinguished of all the people, there is a time for many tales, and a time also for sleep;
sentences.n: He answers: there is time for both. The address is the same line that began his earlier reply. ὥρη μὲν … ὥρη δὲ … (understand ἐστί) is ‘a time for … and a time for …’, and the repeated ὥρη is the point; πολέων is the Ionic genitive plural of πολύς ‘many’, with μύθων ‘tales’, and ὕπνου is ‘sleep’. Unlike his short answer a few lines earlier, this speech is not closed: its opening mark begins Odysseus’s long speech afresh, and it runs on into the story.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἔτ’ ἀκουέμεναί γε λιλαίεαι, οὐκ ἂν ἐγώ γε
τούτων σοι φθονέοιμι καὶ οἰκτρότερ’ ἄλλ’ ἀγορεύειν,
sentences.tr:
ei d’ et’ akouemenai ge lilaieai, ouk an egō ge
toutōn soi phthoneoimi kai oiktroter’ all’ agoreuein,
sentences.l:
but if still to listen you are eager, not I
would begrudge you these, and more pitiable others to tell,
sentences.i: but if you still long to listen, I would not begrudge you these, or to tell you other, more pitiable ones,
sentences.n: He agrees, and the object of his generosity comes in the next unit. εἰ … λιλαίεαι is ‘if you long’, from λιλαίομαι, with the infinitive ἀκουέμεναι ‘to listen’ (the -έμεναι ending is an old infinitive; compare Attic ἀκούειν). οὐκ ἂν … φθονέοιμι is ‘I would not begrudge’, optative with ἄν, with the dative σοι and the genitive τούτων ‘these things’. καὶ οἰκτρότερ’ ἄλλ’ ἀγορεύειν is ‘and to tell other, more pitiable ones’: οἰκτρότερ’ ἄλλ’ is οἰκτρότερα ἄλλα, the comparative of οἰκτρός ‘pitiable’. The sentence runs five lines, so it is cut at the comma, where the apposition begins.

sentences.t:
κήδε’ ἐμῶν ἑτάρων, οἳ δὴ μετόπισθεν ὄλοντο,
οἳ Τρώων μὲν ὑπεξέφυγον στονόεσσαν ἀυτήν,
ἐν νόστῳ δ’ ἀπόλοντο κακῆς ἰότητι γυναικός.
sentences.tr:
kēde’ emōn hetarōn, hoi dē metopisthen olonto,
hoi Trōōn men hypexephygon stonoessan aytēn,
en nostōi d’ apolonto kakēs iotēti gynaikos.
sentences.l:
the sorrows of my companions, who afterward perished,
who the Trojans’ groan-filled battle-cry escaped,
but on the homecoming perished through the evil will of a woman.
sentences.i: the sorrows of my companions, who perished afterward: they escaped the groan-filled battle-cry of the Trojans, but on their homecoming perished through the evil will of a woman.
sentences.n: What the ‘other pitiable things’ are: the sorrows of the men who got through Troy and died on the way home. κήδε’ is κήδεα ‘sorrows’, in apposition to οἰκτρότερ’ ἄλλ’. οἳ δὴ μετόπισθεν ὄλοντο is ‘who perished afterward’, with ὄλοντο the aorist middle of ὄλλυμι without augment. οἳ Τρώων μὲν ὑπεξέφυγον στονόεσσαν ἀυτήν is ‘who escaped the groan-filled battle-cry of the Trojans’: ἀυτή is ‘battle-cry’, στονόεσσα ‘full of groaning’ (στόνος ‘groan’). ἐν νόστῳ is ‘on the homecoming’. κακῆς ἰότητι γυναικός is ‘through the evil will of a woman’: ἰότης is the same ‘will’ as in the gods’ will above, here wicked. The woman is not yet named.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ψυχὰς μὲν ἀπεσκέδασ’ ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ
ἁγνὴ Περσεφόνεια γυναικῶν θηλυτεράων,
ἦλθε δ’ ἐπὶ ψυχὴ Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο
ἀχνυμένη·
sentences.tr:
autar epei psychas men apeskedas’ allydis allēi
hagnē Persephoneia gynaikōn thēlyteraōn,
ēlthe d’ epi psychē Agamemnonos Atreïdao
achnymenē·
sentences.l:
But when the souls, on the one hand, she had scattered this way and that,
pure Persephone, of women, the female ones,
and there came thereupon the soul of Agamemnon, Atreus’ son,
grieving;
sentences.i: But when pure Persephone had scattered the souls of the women this way and that, there came up the soul of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, grieving;
sentences.n: A new scene: the women are dispersed and Agamemnon’s soul arrives. αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ … μέν is ‘but when …’, and ἦλθε δ’ ἐπί is ‘and there came thereupon’, with ἐπί used as an adverb. ψυχάς is ‘souls’, and ἀπεσκέδασ’ is ἀπεσκέδασε, ‘scattered’; ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ is ‘this way and that’. ἁγνή is ‘pure’. γυναικῶν θηλυτεράων is ‘of the women, the female ones’; θηλυτεράων is a comparative in form (θῆλυς ‘female’), but it means no more than ‘female’ here. Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο is ‘of Agamemnon, Atreus’ son’, the patronymic in the genitive -αο. ἀχνυμένη is ‘grieving’, feminine because ψυχή is.

sentences.t:
περὶ δ’ ἄλλαι ἀγηγέραθ’, ὅσσοι ἅμ’ αὐτῷ
οἴκῳ ἐν Αἰγίσθοιο θάνον καὶ πότμον ἐπέσπον.
sentences.tr:
peri d’ allai agēgerath’, hossoi ham’ autōi
oikōi en Aigisthoio thanon kai potmon epespon.
sentences.l:
and around (him) the other (souls) were gathered, as many as with him
in the house of Aegisthus died and met their doom.
sentences.i: and around him were gathered the other souls, all who had died with him in the house of Aegisthus and met their doom.
sentences.n: Those who died with him come round him. περὶ δ’ ἄλλαι ἀγηγέραθ’ is ‘and around (him) the others were gathered’: ἀγηγέραθ’ is ἀγηγέρατο, the pluperfect passive of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, with the final τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ὅσσοι. ἄλλαι is feminine because it agrees with the unexpressed ψυχαί, while ὅσσοι ‘as many as’ is masculine, because the souls are those of men. οἴκῳ ἐν Αἰγίσθοιο is ‘in the house of Aegisthus’, with ἐν between the noun and the genitive. θάνον is the aorist of θνῄσκω without augment. πότμον ἐπέσπον ‘met their doom’ is the phrase Alcinous used of the men who died at Troy.

sentences.t: ἔγνω δ’ αἶψ’ ἔμ’ ἐκεῖνος, ἐπεὶ πίεν αἷμα κελαινόν·
sentences.tr: egnō d’ aips’ em’ ekeinos, epei pien haima kelainon·
sentences.l: And he knew me at once, that one, when he had drunk the dark blood;
sentences.i: He knew me at once, after he had drunk the dark blood;
sentences.n: ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘know, recognise’, αἶψ’ is ‘at once’, and ἐκεῖνος ‘that one’ puts Agamemnon himself in view. ἐπεὶ πίεν αἷμα κελαινόν is ‘when he had drunk the dark blood’; πίεν is the aorist of πίνω without augment. The ἐπεί clause gives the cause: it is the blood that lets him know Odysseus.

sentences.t:
κλαῖε δ’ ὅ γε λιγέως, θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυον εἴβων,
πιτνὰς εἰς ἐμὲ χεῖρας, ὀρέξασθαι μενεαίνων·
sentences.tr:
klaie d’ ho ge ligeōs, thaleron kata dakryon eibōn,
pitnas eis eme cheiras, orexasthai meneainōn·
sentences.l:
and he wept, he, clearly, an abundant tear letting fall,
spreading his hands toward me, to reach, eager;
sentences.i: and he wept in a clear voice, letting abundant tears fall, spreading out his hands toward me, straining to reach me;
sentences.n: He weeps and reaches for Odysseus. κλαῖε is the imperfect ‘wept’, and ὅ γε is ‘he’, the demonstrative with γε. λιγέως is the adverb of λιγύς ‘clear-toned’, ‘in a clear voice’: it describes the sound of the weeping. θαλερὸν δάκρυον is ‘an abundant tear’ (θαλερός from θάλλω ‘flourish’), and κατά belongs with εἴβων: κατά … εἴβων is a tmesis, the preverb standing apart from the verb ‘letting fall’. πιτνάς is the participle of πίτνημι, a by-form of πετάννυμι ‘spread out’, with χεῖρας εἰς ἐμέ ‘his hands toward me’. ὀρέξασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ὀρέγομαι ‘stretch out, reach’, and μενεαίνων is ‘eager, straining’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ οἱ ἔτ’ ἦν ἲς ἔμπεδος οὐδέ τι κῖκυς,
οἵη περ πάρος ἔσκεν ἐνὶ γναμπτοῖσι μέλεσσι.
sentences.tr:
all’ ou gar hoi et’ ēn is empedos oude ti kikys,
hoiē per paros esken eni gnamptoisi melessi.
sentences.l:
But not now for him was there firm force, nor any vigour,
such as there was before in his pliant limbs.
sentences.i: But he no longer had any firm strength or vigour, such as he once had in his supple limbs.
sentences.n: Why he cannot touch Odysseus. ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ is a clipped phrase, ‘but (it was in vain), for …’. οἱ is the dative ‘for him’, so οὐ … οἱ ἔτ’ ἦν is ‘there was no longer for him’. ἲς ἔμπεδος is ‘firm force’ (ἲς ‘force’, ἔμπεδος ‘steadfast’), and κῖκυς is a rare word for ‘vigour’. οἵη περ πάρος ἔσκεν is ‘such as there was before’; ἔσκεν is the iterative imperfect of εἰμί, ‘used to be’. γναμπτοῖσι μέλεσσι is ‘in pliant limbs’ (γναμπτός ‘bent, supple’, μέλεα ‘limbs’), with the dative ending -οισι.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ δάκρυσα ἰδὼν ἐλέησά τε θυμῷ,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδων·
sentences.tr:
ton men egō dakrysa idōn eleēsa te thymōi,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēudōn·
sentences.l:
Him I wept for, seeing him, and pitied in my heart,
and speaking to him, winged words I addressed to him:
sentences.i: Seeing him, I wept and pitied him in my heart, and I spoke to him and addressed him with winged words:
sentences.n: Odysseus’s own reaction. τὸν is ‘him’; δάκρυσα is the aorist of δακρύω ‘weep’, and with an accusative it means ‘weep for’; ἐλέησα is ‘I pitied’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα is the fixed ‘winged words’, and προσηύδων is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’ (Attic προσηύδων).

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε, ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον,
τίς νύ σε κὴρ ἐδάμασσε τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο;
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē kydiste, anax andrōn Agamemnon,
tis ny se kēr edamasse tanēlegeos thanatoio;
sentences.l:
‘Atreus’ son, most glorious, lord of men, Agamemnon,
what death-spirit subdued you, of death that lays-at-length?
sentences.i: ‘Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, which spirit of the death that lays men at length overcame you?
sentences.n: Odysseus’s first words to Agamemnon begin a speech inside his own, so the quotation marks are single. Ἀτρεΐδη, κύδιστε, ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον are four vocatives; κύδιστε is the superlative of κυδρός ‘glorious’, ‘most glorious’. τίς νύ σε κὴρ ἐδάμασσε … is ‘what spirit now subdued you …’: κήρ is a spirit that brings death, νύ ‘now, then’, and ἐδάμασσε the aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue’. τανηλεγέος is of unknown meaning: ‘that lays men out at length’ (from τανύω and λέγω) and ‘bringing long sorrow’ (from ἄλγος) are both ancient guesses, and the first is followed here without being certain.

sentences.t:
ἦε σέ γ’ ἐν νήεσσι Ποσειδάων ἐδάμασσεν
ὄρσας ἀργαλέων ἀνέμων ἀμέγαρτον ἀυτμήν;
sentences.tr:
ēe se g’ en nēessi Poseidaōn edamassen
orsas argaleōn anemōn amegarton aytmēn;
sentences.l:
Was it that you in the ships Poseidon subdued,
having roused of grievous winds the unenviable blast?
sentences.i: Was it Poseidon who overcame you among your ships, by rousing a dreadful blast of grievous winds?
sentences.n: The first of three guesses: the sea. ἦε opens the series, ‘was it … or … or’. Ποσειδάων is the epic form of Poseidon’s name, ἐν νήεσσι ‘among the ships’ (the epic dative plural of νηῦς), and ἐδάμασσεν ‘subdued’. ὄρσας is the aorist participle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. ἀργαλέων ἀνέμων is ‘of grievous winds’. ἀμέγαρτον ἀυτμήν is ‘an ἀμέγαρτος blast’: ἀυτμή is ‘blast, breath’, and ἀμέγαρτος is of uncertain meaning, traditionally ‘not to be envied’ and so ‘dreadful’. ‘Unenviable’ is the literal gloss and ‘dreadful’ the translation.

sentences.l:
Or did hostile men harm you on dry land,
cutting off cattle and the fine flocks of sheep,
or fighting for a city and for women?’
sentences.i: Or did hostile men harm you on dry land, as you were driving off cattle and fine flocks of sheep, or fighting for a city and for women?’
sentences.n: The second and third guesses: enemies on land. ἀνάρσιοι is ‘hostile’; ἐδηλήσαντ’ is the aorist middle of δηλέομαι ‘harm’; ἐπὶ χέρσου is ‘on dry land’. βοῦς περιταμνόμενον is ‘cutting off cattle’: περιτάμνομαι is ‘cut off, drive off (a herd)’, a raider’s word, and the participle agrees with σε ‘you’. πώεα καλά is ‘fine flocks’, with οἰῶν the genitive plural of οἶς ‘sheep’. ἠὲ περὶ πτόλιος μαχεούμενον ἠδὲ γυναικῶν is ‘or fighting about a city and for women’: πτόλις is the old form of πόλις, and μαχεούμενον is the epic form of μαχόμενον. Odysseus’s question ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπε·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, ho de m’ autik’ ameibomenos proseeipe·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he then at once, answering me, addressed me:
sentences.i: So I said, and he answered me at once:
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s reply-formula: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’, ὁ δέ ‘and he’, αὐτίκ’ ‘at once’, and ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπε ‘answering addressed’. The speaker ὁ is explicitly masculine.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
οὔτ’ ἐμέ γ’ ἐν νήεσσι Ποσειδάων ἐδάμασσεν
ὄρσας ἀργαλέων ἀνέμων ἀμέγαρτον ἀυτμήν,
οὔτε μ’ ἀνάρσιοι ἄνδρες ἐδηλήσαντ’ ἐπὶ χέρσου,
sentences.tr:
diogenes Laertiadē, polymēchan’ Odysseu,
out’ eme g’ en nēessi Poseidaōn edamassen
orsas argaleōn anemōn amegarton aytmēn,
oute m’ anarsioi andres edēlēsant’ epi chersou,
sentences.l:
‘Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
neither me in the ships did Poseidon subdue,
having roused of grievous winds the unenviable blast,
nor did hostile men harm me on dry land,
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, Poseidon did not overcome me among my ships by rousing a dreadful blast of grievous winds, nor did hostile men harm me on dry land,
sentences.n: Agamemnon denies the first two guesses in Odysseus’s own words: lines 406–407 repeat the earlier question with the negative οὔτ’ … οὔτε. διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ is ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices’, with Λαερτιάδη the patronymic vocative. οὔτ’ ἐμέ γ’ … οὔτε μ’ … is ‘neither me … nor me’. ἀμέγαρτον ‘unenviable’ is as explained above. The comma after the second οὔτε clause is where the syntax pauses, before ἀλλά ‘but’ gives the true cause.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι Αἴγισθος τεύξας θάνατόν τε μόρον τε
ἔκτα σὺν οὐλομένῃ ἀλόχῳ, οἶκόνδε καλέσσας,
δειπνίσσας, ὥς τίς τε κατέκτανε βοῦν ἐπὶ φάτνῃ.
sentences.tr:
alla moi Aigisthos teuxas thanaton te moron te
ekta syn oulomenēi alochōi, oikonde kalessas,
deipnissas, hōs tis te katektane boun epi phatnēi.
sentences.l:
but Aegisthus, having contrived for me both death and doom,
killed me, with (my) ruinous wife, having called me to his house,
having feasted me, as one slays an ox at the manger.
sentences.i: but Aegisthus contrived death and doom for me, and killed me with my ruinous wife, after calling me to his house and feasting me, as one might slaughter an ox at its manger.
sentences.n: The true cause. ἀλλά ‘but’ answers the two denials. τεύξας is ‘having contrived’ (τεύχω ‘make, contrive’), and θάνατόν τε μόρον τε is the formula ‘both death and doom’, with μόρος properly ‘portion’, one’s allotted end. ἔκτα ‘killed’ is the same short aorist as before. σὺν οὐλομένῃ ἀλόχῳ is ‘with (my) ruinous wife’: the Greek has no ‘my’, and οὐλομένῃ, from ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’, is a curse-word, ‘ruinous, accursed’. οἶκόνδε is ‘to (his) house’, with the -δε of direction, and δειπνίσσας ‘having given a meal’. The last line is the simile of the ox: ὥς τίς τε κατέκτανε is ‘as one kills’ (a general statement in the aorist, with epic τε).

sentences.t: ὣς θάνον οἰκτίστῳ θανάτῳ·
sentences.tr: hōs thanon oiktistōi thanatōi·
sentences.l: So I died by a most pitiable death;
sentences.i: So I died, by a most pitiable death;
sentences.n: ὣς θάνον is ‘so I died’, with θάνον the aorist of θνῄσκω without augment. οἰκτίστῳ is the superlative of οἰκτρός ‘pitiable’, ‘most pitiable’. The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
περὶ δ’ ἄλλοι ἑταῖροι
νωλεμέως κτείνοντο σύες ὣς ἀργιόδοντες,
οἵ ῥά τ’ ἐν ἀφνειοῦ ἀνδρὸς μέγα δυναμένοιο
ἢ γάμῳ ἢ ἐράνῳ ἢ εἰλαπίνῃ τεθαλυίῃ.
sentences.tr:
peri d’ alloi hetairoi
nōlemeōs kteinonto syes hōs argiodontes,
hoi rha t’ en aphneiou andros mega dynamenoio
ē gamōi ē eranōi ē eilapinēi tethaluiēi.
sentences.l:
and around (me) my other companions
unceasingly were being killed, like white-toothed pigs,
which in the house of a rich man, greatly powerful,
(are killed) at a wedding, or a meal of shared contributions, or a flourishing banquet.
sentences.i: and around me my other companions were slaughtered without pause, like white-toothed pigs killed in the house of a rich and powerful man, at a wedding, or a meal where each man brings his share, or a flourishing banquet.
sentences.n: His companions died with him, like pigs at a feast. περὶ δ’ ἄλλοι ἑταῖροι is ‘and around (me) my other companions’; νωλεμέως is ‘unceasingly, without pause’, and κτείνοντο the imperfect passive of κτείνω, ‘were being killed’. σύες ὣς ἀργιόδοντες is ‘like white-toothed pigs’: σύες is the nominative plural of σῦς ‘pig’, and ὣς follows its noun. The relative clause οἵ ῥά τ’ … has no verb, and the sense supplies ‘are killed’. ἀφνειοῦ is ‘rich’, μέγα δυναμένοιο ‘greatly powerful’. The three occasions are γάμῳ ‘a wedding’, ἐράνῳ (a meal to which each guest brings a share) and εἰλαπίνῃ τεθαλυίῃ, ‘a flourishing banquet’, with τεθαλυίῃ the perfect participle of θάλλω ‘thrive’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη μὲν πολέων φόνῳ ἀνδρῶν ἀντεβόλησας,
μουνὰξ κτεινομένων καὶ ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ·
sentences.tr:
ēdē men poleōn phonōi andrōn antebolēsas,
mounax kteinomenōn kai eni kraterēi hysminēi·
sentences.l:
Before now, indeed, at the slaughter of many men you have met,
of men killed singly, and in strong battle;
sentences.i: Before now you have come upon the slaughter of many men, men killed one by one and in strong battle;
sentences.n: Agamemnon compares the scene with what Odysseus has already seen. ἤδη μέν is ‘already, indeed’, with a μέν that the ἀλλά of the next unit answers. ἀντεβόλησας is the aorist of ἀντιβολέω ‘meet, come upon’, with the dative φόνῳ ‘slaughter’. μουνάξ is ‘singly, one by one’ (from μόνος), κτεινομένων ‘of men being killed’, and ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ is ‘in strong battle’ (ὑσμίνη ‘battle’).

sentences.t:
ἀλλά κε κεῖνα μάλιστα ἰδὼν ὀλοφύραο θυμῷ,
ὡς ἀμφὶ κρητῆρα τραπέζας τε πληθούσας
κείμεθ’ ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ, δάπεδον δ’ ἅπαν αἵματι θῦεν.
sentences.tr:
alla ke keina malista idōn olophyrao thymōi,
hōs amphi krētēra trapezas te plēthousas
keimeth’ eni megarōi, dapedon d’ hapan haimati thyen.
sentences.l:
but you would most of all, seeing those things, have lamented in your heart,
how around the mixing-bowl and the tables, full,
we lay in the hall, and the whole floor seethed with blood.
sentences.i: But what you would most have lamented in your heart, had you seen it, is how we lay in the hall around the mixing-bowl and the laden tables, and the whole floor seethed with blood.
sentences.n: What would have shocked Odysseus more: the hall. ἀλλά κε … ὀλοφύραο is ‘but you would have lamented’, the optative of ὀλοφύρομαι ‘lament’ with κε; κεῖνα is ‘those things’, which the clause with ὡς ‘how’ then describes. ἀμφὶ κρητῆρα τραπέζας τε πληθούσας is ‘around the mixing-bowl and the tables, full’: the κρητήρ is the great bowl in which wine was mixed with water, and πληθούσας, from πλήθω, ‘being full’, is ‘laden’. κείμεθ’ is κείμεθα ‘we lay’. θῦεν is the imperfect of θύω ‘rush, seethe’, said of the floor ‘seething’ with blood.

sentences.t:
οἰκτροτάτην δ’ ἤκουσα ὄπα Πριάμοιο θυγατρός,
Κασσάνδρης, τὴν κτεῖνε Κλυταιμνήστρη δολόμητις
ἀμφ’ ἐμοί, αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ ποτὶ γαίῃ χεῖρας ἀείρων
βάλλον ἀποθνήσκων περὶ φασγάνῳ·
sentences.tr:
oiktrotatēn d’ ēkousa opa Priamoio thygatros,
Kassandrēs, tēn kteine Klytaimnēstrē dolomētis
amph’ emoi, autar egō poti gaiēi cheiras aeirōn
ballon apothnēskōn peri phasganōi·
sentences.l:
And most pitiable I heard the voice of Priam’s daughter,
Cassandra, whom killed Clytemnestra of guileful counsel
around me; but I upon the ground my hands lifting
kept casting them, dying, around the sword;
sentences.i: And the most pitiable sound I heard was the voice of Priam’s daughter, Cassandra, whom Clytemnestra of guileful counsel killed at my side; while I, dying around the sword, lifted my hands and let them fall to the ground;
sentences.n: Cassandra’s death, heard by the dying man. οἰκτροτάτην … ὄπα is ‘the most pitiable voice’ (ὄπα is the accusative of ὄψ ‘voice’; οἰκτροτάτην is the superlative of οἰκτρός). τὴν κτεῖνε is ‘whom (she) killed’, with κτεῖνε the unaugmented imperfect of κτείνω. Κλυταιμνήστρη δολόμητις is ‘Clytemnestra of guileful counsel’, the epithet built on δόλος ‘guile’ and μῆτις ‘counsel’; ἀμφ’ ἐμοί is ‘around me, at my side’. In the last clause ποτί is πρός ‘toward’ and most likely goes with βάλλον, the imperfect of βάλλω, ‘kept throwing’; περὶ φασγάνῳ is ‘around the sword’, and the Greek does not say more than that, so the exact picture is left open.

sentences.t:
ἡ δὲ κυνῶπις
νοσφίσατ’, οὐδέ μοι ἔτλη ἰόντι περ εἰς Ἀίδαο
χερσὶ κατ’ ὀφθαλμοὺς ἑλέειν σύν τε στόμ’ ἐρεῖσαι.
sentences.tr:
hē de kynōpis
nosphisat’, oude moi etlē ionti per eis Aidao
chersi kat’ ophthalmous heleein syn te stom’ ereisai.
sentences.l:
but she, dog-faced,
turned away, nor did she bring herself, as I went even to Hades’ (house),
with her hands to close my eyes and to press my mouth together.
sentences.i: but the shameless one turned away, and did not bring herself, even as I went to the house of Hades, to close my eyes with her hands or to press my mouth shut.
sentences.n: She refused the last offices: closing the eyes and mouth was the duty of those near the dying. κυνῶπις, from κύων ‘dog’ and ὤψ ‘face’, is a reproach of shamelessness, ‘dog-faced’ in the literal layer and ‘shameless’ in the other. νοσφίσατ’ is the aorist middle of νοσφίζομαι ‘turn away from’, and οὐδέ μοι ἔτλη is ‘nor did she bring herself’ (ἔτλη, aorist of τλάω). ἰόντι περ εἰς Ἀίδαο is ‘as I went even to Hades’: ἰόντι is a dative participle agreeing with μοι, and Ἀίδαο a genitive with ‘house’ understood. κατ’ ὀφθαλμοὺς ἑλέειν is literally ‘to take down over the eyes’, the idiom for closing them; ἐρεῖσαι is ‘to press’.

sentences.t:
ὣς οὐκ αἰνότερον καὶ κύντερον ἄλλο γυναικός,
ἥ τις δὴ τοιαῦτα μετὰ φρεσὶν ἔργα βάληται·
sentences.tr:
hōs ouk ainoteron kai kynteron allo gynaikos,
hē tis dē toiauta meta phresin erga balētai·
sentences.l:
So there is nothing else more fearsome and more dog-like than a woman,
who such deeds in her wits may cast;
sentences.i: So nothing is more fearsome or more shameless than a woman who takes such deeds into her mind;
sentences.n: Agamemnon draws the moral. ὣς here is the adverb ‘so, in this way’, summing up what he has just told. αἰνότερον and κύντερον are comparatives, ‘more fearsome’ and ‘more dog-like’; κύντερον comes from κύων ‘dog’, the same root as κυνῶπις, so it means ‘more shameless’ and echoes the word just used of Clytemnestra. ἄλλο is ‘anything else’, and γυναικός is the genitive of comparison, ‘than a woman’. ἥ τις … βάληται is ‘whichever one puts’, a general subjunctive; μετὰ φρεσὶν ἔργα βάληται is literally ‘throws deeds among her wits’, that is, takes them into her mind.

sentences.t:
οἷον δὴ καὶ κείνη ἐμήσατο ἔργον ἀεικές,
κουριδίῳ τεύξασα πόσει φόνον.
sentences.tr:
hoion dē kai keinē emēsato ergon aeikes,
kouridiōi teuxasa posei phonon.
sentences.l:
such a deed as she too devised, an unseemly one,
contriving for her wedded husband slaughter.
sentences.i: such an unseemly deed as she too devised, contriving the murder of her wedded husband.
sentences.n: The deed he means. οἷον … ἔργον ἀεικές is ‘such a deed, an unseemly one’, with οἷον ‘of the kind that’ and ἀεικές ‘unseemly’. ἐμήσατο is the aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘devise’, and κουριδίῳ … πόσει is ‘to her wedded husband’ (κουριδίος ‘lawfully wedded’, from κούρη; πόσις ‘husband’). τεύξασα φόνον is ‘contriving murder’, with τεύχω ‘make, contrive’ as above.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ἔφην γε
ἀσπάσιος παίδεσσιν ἰδὲ δμώεσσιν ἐμοῖσιν
οἴκαδ’ ἐλεύσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
ē toi ephēn ge
aspasios paidessin ide dmōessin emoisin
oikad’ eleusesthai·
sentences.i: I had supposed, certainly, that I would come home a welcome sight to my children and my servants;
sentences.n: What he had expected. ἦ τοι ἔφην γε is ‘truly I said’, and ἔφην can also be ‘I supposed’, the sense used in the second layer. ἐλεύσεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἔρχομαι, ‘that I would come’, and οἴκαδ’ is οἴκαδε ‘homeward’, with the -δε of direction. ἀσπάσιος is ‘welcome’, and παίδεσσιν ἰδὲ δμώεσσιν ἐμοῖσιν is ‘to my children and to my servants’, with the -εσσι datives and ἰδέ for καί. The ano teleia sets up the contrast of the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἔξοχα λυγρὰ ἰδυῖα
οἷ τε κατ’ αἶσχος ἔχευε καὶ ἐσσομένῃσιν ὀπίσσω
θηλυτέρῃσι γυναιξί, καὶ ἥ κ’ ἐυεργὸς ἔῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ exocha lygra iduia
hoi te kat’ aischos echeue kai essomenēisin opissō
thēlyterēisi gynaixi, kai hē k’ eyergos eēisin.
sentences.i: But she, who knew grievous things beyond all others, poured shame down upon herself and upon all women yet to come, even the one who does well.
sentences.n: What her deed has done to all women. ἰδυῖα is the perfect participle of οἶδα ‘know’, here ‘versed in’, and ἔξοχα is ‘outstandingly’. οἷ τε is ‘for herself’ (οἷ is the dative of the third-person reflexive), and κατ’ αἶσχος ἔχευε is ‘poured shame down’, a tmesis of κατέχευε, with ἔχευε the aorist of χέω. ἐσσομένῃσιν ὀπίσσω θηλυτέρῃσι γυναιξί is ‘for women yet to come hereafter’: ἐσσομένῃσιν is the future participle of εἰμί, and θηλυτέρῃσι ‘female’, as in the earlier line. καὶ ἥ κ’ ἐυεργὸς ἔῃσιν is ‘even for whichever may be well-working’: ἐυεργός is ‘doing well’, and ἔῃσιν the epic subjunctive of εἰμί (Attic ᾖ).
